query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of a eutectic-forming interlayer element (such as Ni) during processing will enable liquid‐phase assisted interfacial bonding between W and Cu, preventing phase separation and eliminating interfacial voids, thereby enhancing the thermal conductivity of the composite under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite containing either isolated W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix that, upon conventional processing, develops phase separation and voids at the W/Cu interfaces.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor volume fraction of a eutectic-forming element (e.g., nickel) into the composite formulation so that during rapid ultrahigh-temperature sintering a transient liquid phase forms at the W/Cu interface.
generation.conditions: Applied during powder consolidation by rapid liquid-phase assisted sintering under conditions relevant to plasma-facing components joined to Cu-based cooling systems, with subsequent exposure to high heat flux and irradiation (e.g., Ar+, He+, and other ions) representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous Ni-rich interfacial layer (or intermetallic phase) that forms in situ by interdiffusion during processing.
generation.mechanism: The transient liquid phase induced by the eutectic-forming Ni enhances wetting and diffusion at the W/Cu interface, thereby eliminating voids and suppressing phase separation. Upon cooling, the Ni-rich interlayer solidifies into a defect-minimized, chemically bonded bridge that facilitates efficient heat transfer and resists irradiation-induced microstructural degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified composite is expected to display improved interfacial integrity and enhanced thermal conductivity compared to the untreated W–Cu composite, with reduced interfacial resistance under both heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites typically exhibit significant phase separation and interfacial void formation during high-temperature or irradiative cycling, which degrades thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable provided the processing schedule (temperature, heating rate, and time) is controlled to induce transient liquid phase formation without excessive intermetallic growth, and under service conditions where the joint is exposed to high heat flux and irradiation similar to those in tungsten plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in thermal conductivity and optimal Ni content (or processing parameters) are uncertain without experimental calibration; the balance between sufficient liquid-phase formation and avoiding detrimental intermetallic thickening needs verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites via identical rapid sintering processing, one set having a small (e.g., 1–3 wt%) Ni additive intended to form the eutectic-based interlayer and one control set without the additive. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation treatments mimicking service conditions.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure analysis using high-resolution SEM/TEM to assess void formation and phase continuity at the W/Cu interface.
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., by laser flash analysis) before and after thermal/irradiation cycles.
Microhardness and density measurements to confirm structural integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-added composite does not show statistically significant improvement in interfacial integrity (i.e., void elimination and suppression of phase separation) or if its thermal conductivity is not measurably higher than that of the control composite after treatment, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effect of Ti/Ni Coating of Diamond Particles on Microstructure and Properties of High-Entropy Alloy/Diamond Composites

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, an effective way of applying Ti/Ni deposited coating to the surface of diamond single crystal particles by magnetron sputtering was proposed and novel high-entropy alloy (HEA)/diamond composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The results show that the interfacial bonding state of the coated diamond composite is obviously better than that of the uncoated diamond composite. Corresponding mechanical properties such as hardness, density, transverse fracture strength and friction properties of the coated diamond composite were also found to be better than those of the uncoated diamond composite. The effects of interface structure and defects on the mechanical properties of HEA/diamond composites were investigated. The research directions for further improving the structure and properties of high-entropy alloy/diamond composites were proposed. Keywords: high-entropy alloy, diamond, coating, interface, mechanical properties

Rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering of high-entropy ceramic composites

Abstract: High-entropy ceramics and their composites display high mechanical strength and attractive high-temperature stabilities. However, properties like strong covalent bond character and low self-diffusion coefficients make them difficult to get sintered, limiting their mass popularity. Here, we present a rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering strategy and use high-entropy metal diboride/boron carbide composite as a proof of concept. We use a carbon-based heater to fast-heat the composite to around 3000 K, and a small fraction of eutectic liquid was formed at the interface between high-entropy metal diborides and boron carbide. A crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase was generated upon cooling to ameliorate the adhesion between the components. The as-sintered composite presents a high hardness of 36.4 GPa at a load of 0.49 N and 24.4 GPa at a load of 9.8 N. This liquid phase–assisted rapid ultrahigh-temperature strategy can be widely applicable for other ultrahigh-temperature ceramics as well.
